# Conti Ransomware Leaks and Public Attribution Record

## Executive assessment

The supplied public record supports a coherent description of Conti as a commercially organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that combined internally developed malware, specialized personnel, affiliates, and a double-extortion business model. The strongest evidence for this characterization comes from the leaked internal chats summarized by Rapid7 and the Center for Internet Security (CIS). Those sources describe recruitment, salary discussions, departmental specialization, malware testing, procurement of security tools, and reliance on outside parties for functions such as initial access and spamming. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The record also shows that the February 2022 leaks exposed operational, financial, technical, and organizational information. Rapid7 reported that the leak contained approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files, as well as screenshots, discussions of exploits and development processes, and credentials that the researchers expressly warned readers not to use. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) The leak therefore provided unusually direct evidence of cybercrime commercialization, although some messages were encrypted and the identity of the leaker was not established.

The U.S. Rewards for Justice page presents Conti—also called Wizard Spider—as a Russian government-linked RaaS group and identifies five online aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti. This is an official government attribution and reward statement, but its wording is important: the page says the actors are “believed to be linked,” not that it publicly proves a specific legal identity for each alias. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.-a](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The Department of Justice record separately identifies Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko as defendants in Conti-related federal cases. However, the supplied DOJ page does not map those defendants to the five aliases listed by Rewards for Justice. It describes charges and procedural developments, while emphasizing that defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)) Accordingly, the evidence supports a relationship between the defendants and alleged Conti activity as reflected in the charging records, but it does not support assigning any particular alias to any particular defendant.

## Source and evidentiary framework

For clarity, this report assigns the following source identifiers to the supplied materials:

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary role |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Rewards for Justice, “Conti” | Official U.S. government attribution, alias list, threat description, reward notice |
| S2 | Rapid7, “Conti Ransomware Group Internal Chats Leaked Over Russia-Ukraine Conflict” | Technical and organizational analysis of leaked chats |
| S3 | Center for Internet Security, “The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization” | Analysis of Conti’s RaaS structure and commercialization |
| S4 | U.S. Attorney’s Office, Middle District of Tennessee, “Conti Ransomware” | Federal defendant and case information, charges, plea and proceeding records |

The sources do not all make the same type of assertion. S1 is an official government reward announcement and attribution assessment. S2 is a private-sector threat-intelligence analysis based partly on leaked material. S3 is a nonprofit cybersecurity analysis that incorporates the Conti leaks and an MS-ISAC perspective. S4 is an official law-enforcement case page, but it records allegations and procedural events rather than final adjudications for every defendant.

## How public sources describe Conti as an RaaS operation

### Double extortion and monetization

The supplied sources describe Conti as using a double-extortion model. Operators allegedly stole victims’ files and encrypted servers and workstations, then demanded payment. If a victim refused, the stolen information could be sold or published on a site controlled by the actors. Rewards for Justice states that ransom demands varied considerably and could reach $25 million. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.-a](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The RaaS model separated malware development and administration from at least some intrusion activity. CIS explains that RaaS operators lease or provide malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers, commonly using a revenue split described in the article as approximately 70–30. CIS also describes initial access brokers as an important part of this ecosystem because they can sell already established access to victim environments. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

This division of labor increased operational scale. Instead of requiring the core group to perform every intrusion, affiliates or access brokers could supply access, while the central organization focused on software development, support, negotiation, and revenue management. CIS’s conclusion is that commercialization enabled cybercriminals to increase the number of potential victims and to reinvest income into the malware operation. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

### Malware and associated tools

Rewards for Justice associates Conti with the Conti ransomware-as-a-service application and lists Wizard Spider, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader as associated cyberthreat organizations or applications. The page does not state that every listed tool was developed by Conti; rather, it presents them as associated with the threat activity. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.-a](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

Rapid7 reports that Conti used phishing to establish access, discussed malicious documents and delivery logistics, and tested its malware against endpoint-detection products to improve its ability to avoid detection. The same analysis identifies several vulnerabilities associated with Conti activity, including MS17-010-related vulnerabilities, ZeroLogon, PrintNightmare, Log4Shell, and ProxyShell/ProxyLogon vulnerabilities. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The use of Cobalt Strike is especially relevant to the commercialization account. CIS reports that the leaked material indicated Conti allocated $60,000 to obtain a valid Cobalt Strike license and spent several thousand dollars monthly on security and antivirus software for testing. These details portray an organization investing in both offensive tooling and quality assurance rather than operating as a loose collection of opportunistic criminals. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

## What the leaks exposed

### Organizational specialization

The leaks reportedly revealed a structure resembling a technology company. CIS describes internal units or job categories including “Coders,” “Testers,” “Administrators,” “Reverse Engineers,” and “Penetration Testers/Hackers.” Spamming functions were reportedly outsourced. Each business unit had a budget, although funds could be borrowed between units. CIS further reports that an insider estimated the group employed more than 60 people in July 2021, principally coders and testers. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

Rapid7 similarly describes recruitment processes, coding exercises, salary negotiations, product status discussions, and ordinary workplace communications. The reported interview process resembled a conventional technical hiring process, demonstrating that the group attempted to recruit and manage individuals according to specialized skills. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### Development, testing, and adaptation

The communications exposed efforts to improve the ransomware product. Rapid7 reports discussions about encryption of very large files, endpoint-detection evasion, target-specific features, malicious document delivery, and compatibility with newer operating systems. CIS reports that reverse engineers were redirected toward Windows 11 in July 2021. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The practical implication is that Conti’s “product” was treated as an iterative software platform. The group sought to test, update, and adapt its malware to defensive technologies and operating-system changes. This is a supported assessment of operational behavior, not proof that every planned feature was successfully implemented.

### Infrastructure and financial information

Rapid7 states that the leak included screenshots of a Conti control panel showing compromised hosts, operating systems, antivirus products, user rights, and other information about infected assets. The leak also reportedly exposed command-and-control and storage-server access information, usernames, and passwords. Rapid7 did not access the remote systems and warned against doing so. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

Rapid7 further reported that leaked financial information identified a primary Bitcoin address containing more than $2 billion as of February 28, 2022. Because the supplied article characterizes this as information revealed by the chats and does not provide an independent blockchain-verification methodology in the excerpt, the figure should be treated as a reported leak-derived estimate rather than an independently established balance. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### Political conflict and operational disruption

The leak followed Conti’s public expression of support for the Russian government after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Rapid7 reports that some members sided with Ukraine, creating internal conflict, and that a subsequent message revised the group’s position by condemning the war and threatening retaliation only if Russian critical infrastructure were targeted. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

Rapid7 assessed that Conti’s infrastructure takedowns after the disclosure did not immediately eliminate the threat. Its researchers observed a resumption of normal operations by March 9, 2022. CIS later reported that the larger Conti platform shut down and fragmented into smaller units in 2022, with the data-leak and negotiation infrastructure subsequently ceasing operation. These accounts are not necessarily inconsistent: the first concerns short-term operational resilience after the leak, while the second describes later dismantling and fragmentation. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

## Public attribution and law-enforcement record

### Government attribution and aliases

Rewards for Justice offers up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons who, while acting at the direction or control of a foreign government, participate in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The page identifies five aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—as actors believed to be linked to Conti. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.-a](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The same page characterizes Conti/Wizard Spider as Russian government-linked and says Conti targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. It reports more than 1,000 ransomware operations against U.S. and international critical infrastructure and more than 400 victimized organizations worldwide, including more than 290 in the United States. These are figures presented by Rewards for Justice; the supplied material does not provide an independent methodology or case-by-case victim list, so they should be attributed to the government page rather than treated as independently verified totals. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.-a](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

### Federal defendants and procedural status

The DOJ page identifies two federal case numbers and five defendants. Case 3:23-CR-00092 names Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. Case 3:23-CR-00088 names Oleksii Lytvynenko. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

According to the page, the four defendants in the first case were charged in September 2023 with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Lytvynenko was charged in November 2025 with conspiracy to deploy Conti, a ransomware variant that infected computers and networks and encrypted data. The page states that Lytvynenko entered a guilty plea to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, on June 10, 2026, pursuant to a plea agreement. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

The supplied DOJ record does not establish that all five defendants were convicted of all described conduct, nor does it identify the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” or “Dandis” as belonging to any named defendant. That distinction is essential. The law-enforcement record establishes named defendants, charges, and one reported guilty plea; Rewards for Justice establishes an official alias-based attribution request; the supplied evidence does not bridge those two sets of identities.

## Contradictions, limitations, and confidence assessment

The evidence is strongest on Conti’s organizational model and operational practices, because Rapid7 and CIS both independently describe specialization, recruitment, testing, outsourcing, and commercialization. Confidence is also high that U.S. authorities publicly associate Conti with the five listed aliases and that federal prosecutors brought Conti-related charges against the named defendants.

Confidence is lower for specific financial figures, the exact relationship between Conti and Russian state actors, and the identity of the individuals behind the aliases. Rewards for Justice uses the term “Russian government-linked,” while Rapid7 reports that one leaked conversation indicated FSB involvement in part of Conti’s funding and interest in information concerning Bellingcat and Alexei Navalny. Rapid7 presents this as an indication from a conversation, not as a judicially established finding. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The principal conclusion is therefore that the public record supports a commercially structured and highly capable RaaS operation, exposed in unusual detail by the 2022 leaks, and later addressed through official attribution and criminal proceedings. It does not support a complete identity-resolution chart connecting every alias, leak username, and defendant.

## Structured findings

| Question | Answer | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Was Conti described as RaaS? | Yes. The sources describe malware developers, affiliates, revenue sharing, outsourced access, and double extortion. | High |
| What did the leaks reveal? | Specialized departments, recruitment, budgets, testing, development priorities, infrastructure, credentials, and financial information. | High, subject to leak limitations |
| Did the leaks prove Conti’s exact membership? | No. They exposed usernames and at least one alleged developer, but the leaker’s identity and complete membership were not established. | High |
| Were aliases publicly linked to Conti? | Yes, Rewards for Justice lists five aliases as believed to be linked to Conti. | High as an official assessment |
| Were aliases mapped to DOJ defendants? | Not in the supplied sources. | High |
| Were defendants convicted? | The supplied record reports charges against several defendants and a guilty plea by Lytvynenko to one count, but not final adjudications for all defendants. | High |

infrastructure as a result of the chat disclosure. At that time, we assessed that due to their sophisticated capability, deep funding, and quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021, they remained an active and significant threat. As of March 9, 2022, our threat intelligence team has observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti. On February 27, Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti – a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year . Ahead of the chat log disclosures, Conti pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. However, a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. Two days later, Conti posted a second message revising their statement to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted. At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the “AnonFiles” website, containing 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete. The remaining files contained internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes. On February 28 and March 1, a bevy of additional files were posted, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. Among both sets of leaked messages, there were a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts. Additionally, user @ContiLeaks shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files. However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so. @ContiLeaks also shared a file that they purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” @ContiLeaks did, however, name one alleged Conti developer, providing their email address and Github. The scale of the leaked information suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. Conti is a business – and a well-funded one Much of the discussion within the chat logs concerns fairly mundane things – interviewing potential operators of the group, payment for services, out-of-office messages, gossip, and discussions of products. Based on the leaked chats, the Conti interview process actually looks a lot like a standard technical interview, with coding exercises to be performed hosted on public code repositories, salary negotiations, and the status of ongoing products. In addition to other financial information related to specific actors, the leaked chats have revealed Conti’s primary Bitcoin address, which contains over two billion USD as of February 28, 2022. Moreover, a conversation on April 9, 2021 between “mango” and “johnyboy77” indicates Russian FSB involvement in some portion of their funding and that the FSB were interested in files from the media outlet Bellingcat on “Navalny” – an apparent reference to Alexei Navalny, the currently imprisoned opposition leader in Russia. Conti development Conti seems to operate much like a software company – the chat logs disclose concerns with the development of specific features for targets and a particular difficulty in encrypting very large files. The Conti team also attempted to get demos of popular endpoint detection software with the intent to develop their malware to avoid detection. Two of the actors, “lemur” and “terry” shared phishing templates (included verbatim in Appendix B at the end of this post) to be used against potential targets. Conti gains initial access in many ways, with phishing a popular line of attack due in part to its relatively high efficacy and low cost. Conti often uses phishing emails to establish a presence on targeted networks. A screenshot of the Conti control panel was also leaked, showing a number of compromised hosts and a breakdown of the operating systems, antiviruses, user rights, and detailed information about the infected assets. Further discussions detailed the use of infrastructure against targets, disclosing a number of both known and unknown Conti command and control domains. At the time of this post, only a small number of the previously unknown command and control domains appear to be active. Conversations between two operators, “Stern” and “Bentley” discuss the use of third parties for malicious documents, favoring certain providers over others. They also discuss logistics for how to deliver ransomware without being detected by dynamic analysis. In a conversation between the two back in June of 2021, Stern discloses that Conti wants to start their own cryptocurrency but does not know who to work with. There is no evidence that anything came of this desire, and Conti continues to use Bitcoin for their ransoms. Other groups assert they are strictly business In stark contrast to Conti, other groups have made it clear to the public that despite their “business model,” they take no public stance on this crisis. LockBit is remaining aloof from the conflict and made it clear that they intend to operate as usual. Although it is believed that LockBit is a Russian organization, they assert that “we are all simple and peaceful people, we are all Earthlings,” and “for us it is just business and we are all apolitical.” Another ransomware group, ALPHV, claims to be “extremely saddened” by Conti’s pledge of support and condemns Conti. Their message concludes, “The Internet, and even more so its dark side, is not the place for politics.” Rumors of Conti’s demise have been greatly exaggerated Conti’s payment and “support” portal is still live, even following the infighting and leaks. Conti has repeatedly proven to be one of the most capable ransomware actors and these chats indicate that the group is well-organized and still very well-funded despite the schism. Any suggestion that these leaks spell the end for Conti is overstated, and we expect that Conti will continue to be a powerful player in the ransomware space. What you can do We are keeping an eye on dark web activity related to Conti and other ransomware groups and want to reiterate the following steps for protecting yourself from ransomware: User education, especially related to well-crafted phishing campaigns Asset and vulnerability management, including reducing your external attack surface Multi-factor authentication Additionally, it is worth ensuring that you are well-guarded against the exploits and malware commonly used by Conti (vulnerabilities provided in Appendix A at the end of this post). Furthermore, security teams should also take some time to review CISA’s recent report on the group. For further discussion on how to protect yourself from ransomware, see our ransomware prevention solution . Verizon's DBIR reported that 2021-2022 saw a 13% increase, approximately the same level of growth observed in the last five years combined. Verizon's researchers took a closer look at this trend and unearthed some useful context. First, they found that ransomware had been present in about 70% of malware breaches over the previous year. Approximately two in five ransomware incidents used desktop sharing software and involved a confidentiality compromise with respect to the CIA Triad . Slightly fewer (35%) leveraged email as an attack vector. What's Behind The Rise in Ransomware? An important cause of ransomware's growth is the shift towards commercialization of cybercrime. Indeed, many of the most prolific cybercriminal groups have undergone significant changes in operations to scale efforts and expand revenue. In several instances, public reporting has shown these groups incorporating divisions previously associated with legitimate corporations including HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment. Beyond these structures, likely the most significant trend has been the shift to Ransomware as a Service (RaaS), which has seen groups lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers (often in a 70-30 split). The below graphic depicts the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail. Source: Alan Liska, Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover. Several sources of evidence point to cybercrime's growing commercialization but none as explicitly as the recent Conti leaks. Let’s examine what insights it offered below. Overview of Conti RaaS Conti was a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up. It also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot . Conti ransom note template (Source: Bleeping Computer ) Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Conti operators announced their "full support" for Russia. Just a few days following this commitment, a Twitter account dubbed " Contileaks " dumped an archive of chat messages taken from Conti's internal communications dating back to the beginning of 2021, as reported by KrebsonSecurity . It also published additional internal chats from 2020. In the months that followed, Conti's handlers began dismantling their operations. In May 2022 , Bleeping Computer wrote that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members. It was about a month after that when the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure. Findings of the Conti Leaks The Conti leaks have provided several important insights into how a major RaaS group carries out its operations. These include how Conti ran its "office" and how it worked to improve its "product." Distinct Employees with Distinct Goals In the second part of his investigation on the Conti leaks, KrebsonSecurity revealed that Conti's handlers divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. For example, it hired programmers as "Coders" to write malicious code and integrate different technologies, while it relied on "Testers" to validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies. The operation also had "Administrators," "Reverse Engineers," and "Penetration Testers/Hackers" working internally, with spamming functions contracted outside the organization. Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another. According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021. That number didn't remain consistent, however, as the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. Streamlined Operations to Improve Their 'Product' The third installment of KrebsonSecurity's analysis revealed that the Conti gang took several steps to improve its "product" on an ongoing basis. These initiatives included the following: Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool. Budgeting several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the "Testers" could use for their evaluations. Redefining the focus of the "Reverse Engineers" in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time. The MS-ISAC Perspective on the Conti Leaks To get more insight into the Conti leaks, we sat down with the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) team at the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC). Here's what they had to say. How does commercialization help malicious actors like Conti's operators? Organized ransomware groups operating in a corporate structure allow cybercriminals to conduct highly impactful attacks at scale. For example, instead of expending time and resources on gaining initial access to a victim’s environment, a ransomware group can outsource this work by purchasing already established access from IABs. As a result, ransomware affiliates tasked with conducting attacks are able to increase their number of victims, creating a more dangerous cyber threat landscape for network defenders. Operating through affiliates offers several benefits to the RaaS operator. Principally, because they're not conducting intrusions themselves, they're able to offload risk and dramatically increase the number of potential targets, as there's theoretically no limit to the number of affiliates who can carry out these intrusions. This allows the developers to focus efforts and capital on developing and retooling their software, thereby reinvesting in the enterprise. Has the MS-ISAC seen evidence of cybercrime's commercialization in the daily work of supporting members? If so, what has this looked like? Yes, the MS-ISAC regularly receives reporting about SLTT ransomware attacks involving sophisticated RaaS groups like Conti. From mid-2020 through January 2022, for instance, 22 Conti-related SLTT ransomware attacks were reported to the MS-ISAC, impacting organizations ranging from municipal governments to education facilities. Open-source reporting indicates that the “Conti group” is also tied to the Ryuk ransomware variant, which impacted an additional 89 SLTT government entities from late 2018 through mid-2021. To this day, other RaaS groups continue to attack SLTT governments, including at least 23 ransomware attacks associated with the LockBit 2.0 variant since August 2021. Where does cybercrime's commercialization put an emphasis for the future? I would say it only increases the victim set. Ultimately, there's no silver bullet against ransomware. But SLTTs can still do their best to have their bases covered and put themselves in the best position to prevent and react to breaches when they occur. That means becoming members of the MS-ISAC so they can receive our products, leverage our resources, and deploy appropriate protections. For our team, we need to watch closely for shifts in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that could catch members by surprise, and we need to provide the timely intelligence and guidance that will help them proactively defend their networks. If threat actors evolve, we need to, as well. This also includes things like bolstering partnerships that allow us to share timely intel with members. The Center for Internet Security and the MS-ISAC understand the formidable threat RaaS groups present to SLTTs. They offer services and resources to help organizations better defend themselves. These include no-cost services like Malicious Domain Blocking and Reporting (MDBR), which prevents IT systems from connecting to harmful web domains and thereby helps to limit infections related to known malware, ransomware, phishing, and other cyber threats. A robust ransomware defense should also involve some form of endpoint security solution such as the CIS Endpoint Security Services (ESS), which is available to SLTTs through a partnership with CrowdStrike. Finally, the threat underscores the importance for SLTTs to implement the cybersecurity best practices found in the CIS Critical Security Controls , which are designed to prevent all types of cyber attacks. Defending Against Ransomware Like Conti The CTI team's thoughts on the Conti leaks point to an important truth about ransomware. Certainly, some attackers have taken it upon themselves in recent years to restructure as RaaS operations and commercialize their business functions. But for all its innovations, ransomware's aims have not fundamentally changed as a threat. Its purpose still revolves around denying access to files by encrypting infected machines. Subsequently, MS-ISAC members can use the solutions identified by the CTI team along with these resources to strengthen their defenses against ransomware going forward. Conti (also known as Wizard Spider), is a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group that has targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. As of March 9, 2022, our threat intelligence team has observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti. On February 27, Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti – a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year . Ahead of the chat log disclosures, Conti pledged their support for the Russian Government following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. However, a number of members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. Two days later, Conti posted a second message revising their statement to condemn the war and to strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure is targeted. At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was released on the “AnonFiles” website, containing 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files. However, some of the messages were encrypted and could not be read, so the information provided is necessarily incomplete. The remaining files contained internal Conti communications, screenshots of tools, and discussions of their exploits and design processes. On February 28 and March 1, a bevy of additional files were posted, along with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. Among both sets of leaked messages, there were a number of usernames and passwords for a variety of accounts. Additionally, user @ContiLeaks shared access details for a number of alleged Conti command and control servers, plus storage servers for stolen files. However, we have not accessed any of the data necessitating access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and we strongly recommend against doing so. @ContiLeaks also shared a file that they purport to be the source code for the Conti ransomware but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” @ContiLeaks did, however, name one alleged Conti developer, providing their email address and Github. The scale of the leaked information suggests that the leaker is likely either a very senior member of the group or a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. Conti is a business – and a well-funded one Much of the discussion within the chat logs concerns fairly mundane things – interviewing potential operators of the group, payment for services, out-of-office messages, gossip, and discussions of products. Based on the leaked chats, the Conti interview process actually looks a lot like a standard technical interview, with coding exercises to be performed hosted on public code repositories, salary negotiations, and the status of ongoing products. In addition to other financial information related to specific actors, the leaked chats have revealed Conti’s primary Bitcoin address, which contains over two billion USD as of February 28, 2022. Moreover, a conversation on April 9, 2021 between “mango” and “johnyboy77” indicates Russian FSB involvement in some portion of their funding and that the FSB were interested in files from the media outlet Bellingcat on “Navalny” – an apparent reference to Alexei Navalny, the currently imprisoned opposition leader in Russia. Conti development Conti seems to operate much like a software company – the chat logs disclose concerns with the development of specific features for targets and a particular difficulty in encrypting very large files. The Conti team also attempted to get demos of popular endpoint detection software with the intent to develop their malware to avoid detection. Two of the actors, “lemur” and “terry” shared phishing templates (included verbatim in Appendix B at the end of this post) to be used against potential targets. Conti gains initial access in many ways, with phishing a popular line of attack due in part to its relatively high efficacy and low cost. Conti often uses phishing emails to establish a presence on targeted networks. A screenshot of the Conti control panel was also leaked, showing a number of compromised hosts and a breakdown of the operating systems, antiviruses, user rights, and detailed information about the infected assets. Further discussions detailed the use of infrastructure against targets, disclosing a number of both known and unknown Conti command and control domains. At the time of this post, only a small number of the previously unknown command and control domains appear to be active. Conversations between two operators, “Stern” and “Bentley” discuss the use of third parties for malicious documents, favoring certain providers over others. They also discuss logistics for how to deliver ransomware without being detected by dynamic analysis. In a conversation between the two back in June of 2021, Stern discloses that Conti wants to start their own cryptocurrency but does not know who to work with. There is no evidence that anything came of this desire, and Conti continues to use Bitcoin for their ransoms. Other groups assert they are strictly business In stark contrast to Conti, other groups have made it clear to the public that despite their “business model,” they take no public stance on this crisis. LockBit is remaining aloof from the conflict and made it clear that they intend to operate as usual. Although it is believed that LockBit is a Russian organization, they assert that “we are all simple and peaceful people, we are all Earthlings,” and “for us it is just business and we are all apolitical.” Another ransomware group, ALPHV, claims to be “extremely saddened” by Conti’s pledge of support and condemns Conti. Their message concludes, “The Internet, and even more so its dark side, is not the place for politics.” Rumors of Conti’s demise have been greatly exaggerated Conti’s payment and “support” portal is still live, even following the infighting and leaks. Conti has repeatedly proven to be one of the most capable ransomware actors and these chats indicate that the group is well-organized and still very well-funded despite the schism. Any suggestion that these leaks spell the end for Conti is overstated, and we expect that Conti will continue to be a powerful player in the ransomware space. What you can do We are keeping an eye on dark web activity related to Conti and other ransomware groups and want to reiterate the following steps for protecting yourself from ransomware: User education, especially related to well-crafted phishing campaigns Asset and vulnerability management, including reducing your external attack surface Multi-factor authentication Additionally, it is worth ensuring that you are well-guarded against the exploits and malware commonly used by Conti (vulnerabilities provided in Appendix A at the end of this post). Furthermore, security teams should also take some time to review CISA’s recent report on the group. Verizon's DBIR reported that 2021-2022 saw a 13% increase, approximately the same level of growth observed in the last five years combined. Verizon's researchers took a closer look at this trend and unearthed some useful context. First, they found that ransomware had been present in about 70% of malware breaches over the previous year. Approximately two in five ransomware incidents used desktop sharing software and involved a confidentiality compromise with respect to the CIA Triad . Slightly fewer (35%) leveraged email as an attack vector. What's Behind The Rise in Ransomware? An important cause of ransomware's growth is the shift towards commercialization of cybercrime. Indeed, many of the most prolific cybercriminal groups have undergone significant changes in operations to scale efforts and expand revenue. In several instances, public reporting has shown these groups incorporating divisions previously associated with legitimate corporations including HR departments with recruiters, finance and accounting, as well as negotiators to coordinate ransom payment. Beyond these structures, likely the most significant trend has been the shift to Ransomware as a Service (RaaS), which has seen groups lease out malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers (often in a 70-30 split). The below graphic depicts the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail. Source: Alan Liska, Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover. Several sources of evidence point to cybercrime's growing commercialization but none as explicitly as the recent Conti leaks. Let’s examine what insights it offered below. Overview of Conti RaaS Conti was a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up. It also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot . Conti ransom note template (Source: Bleeping Computer ) Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Conti operators announced their "full support" for Russia. Just a few days following this commitment, a Twitter account dubbed " Contileaks " dumped an archive of chat messages taken from Conti's internal communications dating back to the beginning of 2021, as reported by KrebsonSecurity . It also published additional internal chats from 2020. In the months that followed, Conti's handlers began dismantling their operations. In May 2022 , Bleeping Computer wrote that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, gaining even greater mobility (and evasion from law enforcement) for its members. It was about a month after that when the RaaS operation shut down its data leaks and negotiation infrastructure. Findings of the Conti Leaks The Conti leaks have provided several important insights into how a major RaaS group carries out its operations. These include how Conti ran its "office" and how it worked to improve its "product." Distinct Employees with Distinct Goals In the second part of his investigation on the Conti leaks, KrebsonSecurity revealed that Conti's handlers divided their operations into several business units and brought on staff with specific skill sets. For example, it hired programmers as "Coders" to write malicious code and integrate different technologies, while it relied on "Testers" to validate how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies. The operation also had "Administrators," "Reverse Engineers," and "Penetration Testers/Hackers" working internally, with spamming functions contracted outside the organization. Each of those departments had its own budget, though business units were able to borrow funds from one another. According to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people – mostly Coders and Testers – in July 2021. That number didn't remain consistent, however, as the group sometimes let people go following internal security breaches. Streamlined Operations to Improve Their 'Product' The third installment of KrebsonSecurity's analysis revealed that the Conti gang took several steps to improve its "product" on an ongoing basis. These initiatives included the following: Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration testing and reconnaissance tool. Budgeting several thousand dollars each month to pay for security and antivirus software that the "Testers" could use for their evaluations. Redefining the focus of the "Reverse Engineers" in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, Microsoft's newest operating system at the time. The MS-ISAC Perspective on the Conti Leaks To get more insight into the Conti leaks, we sat down with the Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) team at the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC). Here's what they had to say. How does commercialization help malicious actors like Conti's operators? Organized ransomware groups operating in a corporate structure allow cybercriminals to conduct highly impactful attacks at scale. For example, instead of expending time and resources on gaining initial access to a victim’s environment, a ransomware group can outsource this work by purchasing already established access from IABs. As a result, ransomware affiliates tasked with conducting attacks are able to increase their number of victims, creating a more dangerous cyber threat landscape for network defenders. Operating through affiliates offers several benefits to the RaaS operator. Principally, because they're not conducting intrusions themselves, they're able to offload risk and dramatically increase the number of potential targets, as there's theoretically no limit to the number of affiliates who can carry out these intrusions. This allows the developers to focus efforts and capital on developing and retooling their software, thereby reinvesting in the enterprise. Has the MS-ISAC seen evidence of cybercrime's commercialization in the daily work of supporting members? If so, what has this looked like? Yes, the MS-ISAC regularly receives reporting about SLTT ransomware attacks involving sophisticated RaaS groups like Conti. From mid-2020 through January 2022, for instance, 22 Conti-related SLTT ransomware attacks were reported to the MS-ISAC, impacting organizations ranging from municipal governments to education facilities. Open-source reporting indicates that the “Conti group” is also tied to the Ryuk ransomware variant, which impacted an additional 89 SLTT government entities from late 2018 through mid-2021. To this day, other RaaS groups continue to attack SLTT governments, including at least 23 ransomware attacks associated with the LockBit 2.0 variant since August 2021. Where does cybercrime's commercialization put an emphasis for the future? I would say it only increases the victim set. Ultimately, there's no silver bullet against ransomware. But SLTTs can still do their best to have their bases covered and put themselves in the best position to prevent and react to breaches when they occur. That means becoming members of the MS-ISAC so they can receive our products, leverage our resources, and deploy appropriate protections. For our team, we need to watch closely for shifts in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that could catch members by surprise, and we need to provide the timely intelligence and guidance that will help them proactively defend their networks. If threat actors evolve, we need to, as well. This also includes things like bolstering partnerships that allow us to share timely intel with members. The Center for Internet Security and the MS-ISAC understand the formidable threat RaaS groups present to SLTTs. They offer services and resources to help organizations better defend themselves. These include no-cost services like Malicious Domain Blocking and Reporting (MDBR), which prevents IT systems from connecting to harmful web domains and thereby helps to limit infections related to known malware, ransomware, phishing, and other cyber threats. A robust ransomware defense should also involve some form of endpoint security solution such as the CIS Endpoint Security Services (ESS), which is available to SLTTs through a partnership with CrowdStrike. Finally, the threat underscores the importance for SLTTs to implement the cybersecurity best practices found in the CIS Critical Security Controls , which are designed to prevent all types of cyber attacks. Defending Against Ransomware Like Conti The CTI team's thoughts on the Conti leaks point to an important truth about ransomware. Certainly, some attackers have taken it upon themselves in recent years to restructure as RaaS operations and commercialize their business functions. But for all its innovations, ransomware's aims have not fundamentally changed as a threat. Its purpose still revolves around denying access to files by encrypting infected machines. Subsequently, MS-ISAC members can use the solutions identified by the CTI team along with these resources to strengthen their defenses against ransomware going forward.
